nameStory: Corn speedwell gets its name from its habit of growing as a weed in cornfields and other cultivated crops. The 'speedwell' part comes from an old blessing meaning 'farewell and good fortune on your journey' - perhaps because this little plant seems to wish travelers well as it grows along roadsides and paths.
description: Corn speedwell is a tiny annual wildflower that most people overlook, even though it's incredibly common throughout New England. This low-growing plant rarely reaches more than 6 inches tall and forms small mats or patches in disturbed soil. Its most notable features are clusters of minuscule blue flowers and small, oval leaves that feel slightly fuzzy to the touch. Despite being considered a weed, it's actually quite charming when you take a closer look.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny blue flowers, barely 1/8 inch across, with four petals and white centers - you'll need to look closely or use a magnifying glass to appreciate their delicate beauty

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, with a soft, slightly fuzzy texture and visible teeth along the edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling annual that forms small patches close to the ground, with multiple branching stems that feel somewhat sticky when handled

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Heart-shaped seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny seeds - the capsules have a distinctive notched appearance at the top

habitat: Look for corn speedwell in disturbed soils like garden beds, agricultural fields, vacant lots, and along roadsides throughout New England. It thrives in sunny to partially shaded areas with compacted or recently tilled soil. You'll often find it growing alongside other small weeds like chickweed and dandelions in lawns, pathways, and cultivated areas.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin blooming in late spring with their first flush of tiny blue flowers. This is when the plants are most noticeable and easiest to identify.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming throughout summer, producing multiple generations of flowers and seeds. Plants may look stressed during hot, dry periods but quickly recover after rain.
seasonality.fall: Later generations continue flowering into early fall, with seed capsules becoming more prominent. Plants begin to decline as cooler weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring. No above-ground parts remain visible.

funFact: Corn speedwell can complete its entire life cycle - from seed to flower to new seeds - in just 5-6 weeks, which means it can squeeze in multiple generations per growing season and quickly colonize newly disturbed ground.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small speedwells, especially thyme-leaved speedwell, but corn speedwell has distinctly fuzzy, oval leaves while thyme-leaved speedwell has smooth, more rounded leaves. Remember: fuzzy leaves = corn speedwell, smooth leaves = thyme-leaved speedwell.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being labeled a 'weed,' corn speedwell is actually a beneficial plant that provides nectar for tiny beneficial insects and helps prevent soil erosion in disturbed areas. It's also edible and has been used in folk medicine, though it's too small to be of much culinary interest.
compareHints: Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus. Bird's-eye speedwell has larger, more colorful flowers, while American brooklime grows much taller and prefers wet areas. Heath speedwell forms more extensive mats and has a more prostrate growth habit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
